Rail & roads · Angola

Structure registers along Angola's railways and logistics corridors

A dated register of the structures, fields and tracks along the line, measured from the axis or the reserve boundary you give us, to plan works, servitudes and resettlement and to record what changed after floods and erosion. A person reviews every result before it reaches you.

Request a proposal See sample outputs

The problem

A railway draws building to both sides

A line under rehabilitation or a new branch brings work, trade and stations. It also brings houses, stalls and fields close to the track, inside the strip that works and operations need to keep clear.

On rail and road corridors, land changes between one phase of works and the next. A reopened embankment, a new halt or a level crossing draws building; a flood carries soil away and changes the ground by the bridges. When the works or resettlement team arrives, it needs to know what was there and since when, and there is rarely a dated record to hand it.

AfriScan builds that record from imagery: the structures inside each band, with their distance to the track axis and the date of the image, and the change between surveys. For lenders and independent monitors, it is dated evidence between site visits.

Structures in the corridor

Each structure a reviewer confirms, with its distance to the axis or the reserve boundary, its band, its coordinates and its kilometre point.

Before the works

A register on a known date, before rehabilitation starts or public utility is declared, as the baseline for servitudes and resettlement.

After floods and erosion

Ground change along the line after an event, so field teams start with the worst-hit stretches.

The strips in the law

What Angola’s Land Law reserves along transport routes

A summary of published rules as of 27 September 2026, with sources. It is not legal advice.

Article 27 of Lei n.º 9/04 of 9 November 2004 (the Land Law) includes several strips along transport routes among its partial reserves:

Route Strip in the Land Law Article 27(7)
Public-interest railways and stations “uma faixa de protecção confinante em cada eixo da via”, with no width set in the article (f)
Motorways and four-lane roads 30 m on each side (g)
Provincial roads 30 m (h)
Secondary and municipal roads 15 m (h)

Uses that do not collide with the reserve’s purpose are allowed (paragraph 6), and reserves are constituted by the Government (paragraph 2). Land the State does not own enters a reserve only by expropriation or administrative servitude, and fair compensation is always due (paragraphs 9–10). Because the law sets no rail width, the register measures the width set by the concessionaire, the project owner or the impact study.

Rehabilitation and new branches

A baseline before the works, and tracking during them

Before the works. A register of the structures inside each band on a known date, before works start or public utility is declared. In expropriation by zones or alignments, compensation for property outside the first zone counts the necessary improvements made between the declaration of public utility and the taking of possession (Lei n.º 1/21, article 33), so dated registers on both dates help separate what existed from what came later.

Branches and reroutes. For a new branch or a realignment, we count the structures within each width along the alternatives, to show which one touches fewer homes and fields.

During the works. Scheduled re-surveys show earthworks progress, camps and new access roads, and new structures by the line, for the works team and for the lender’s independent monitor.

After the works. A final survey records the corridor as it was left, as a reference for operations.

We build the same registers along pipeline corridors in Angola.

Resettlement

The cut-off date, on dated imagery

On projects financed by development lenders, the lender applies standards such as IFC Performance Standard 5 or the World Bank’s Environmental and Social Standard 5, and the census cut-off date decides who is eligible for compensation. Angola’s expropriation law, Lei n.º 1/21, leaves forced vacating and “realojamento” (resettlement) operations to a separate instrument (article 2(2)–(3)).

A register of the structures on the cut-off date, built from dated imagery, supports IFC Performance Standard 5 cut-off-date records and shows what appeared afterwards. It does not take the place of the census, the asset inventory or the consultation with households, which stay with the project. The environmental impact assessment procedure is in Decreto Presidencial n.º 117/20, and the register comes as layers the ESIA team can use in its own maps.

Resettlement cut-off-date baselines

Floods and erosion

After the rains, before the field team

When a flood reaches the line, post-event imagery shows where the water went, where soil was washed out and where the ground changed around bridges and embankments. The field team gets a map of the worst-hit stretches and starts there.

Optical imagery cannot see through cloud, and the rainy season delays it. Radar shows larger changes even under rainy-season cloud, and a terrain model helps pick out stretches on steep ground or in flood-prone areas before works begin. Terrain, flood and post-event mapping

Where a stretch needs more detail than satellite imagery gives, we propose a drone survey, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires, starting with ANAC’s special authorisation. Drone law in Angola

What you receive

A register by kilometre, ready for GIS

  • Each structure with an ID, its distance to the axis, its band, its kilometre point and its coordinates.
  • Each 500 m segment rated for encroachment density, so teams know where to concentrate.
  • Change between surveys, with before-and-after views and the capture date of each image where the source gives one.
  • A PDF report in Portuguese or English, and GIS layers in GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Dated registers of structures in the corridor, reviewed by a person
  • Route comparison for branches and realignments
  • Tracking of works and earthworks between surveys
  • Change mapping after floods
  • Drone surveys of flagged stretches, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires

What we don’t

  • Engineering inspection of track, bridges or embankments
  • Household census or asset inventory
  • Identify or follow people or vehicles
  • Decide whether a structure is authorised
  • Field or drone work in Cabinda outside the city, or in the Lundas

Frequently asked questions

How wide is a railway's protection strip in Angola?

The Land Law lists public-interest railways and their stations among its partial reserves, “observando-se uma faixa de protecção confinante em cada eixo da via” (with an adjoining protection strip along the line; Lei n.º 9/04, article 27(7)(f)), but that article sets no width. We measure the width the concessionaire or project owner specifies, or several widths in one survey, up to six distances.

And roads?

The same law sets a 30 m strip on each side of motorways and four-lane roads (article 27(7)(g)), 30 m for provincial roads and 15 m for secondary and municipal roads (article 27(7)(h)). The register measures each structure from the road axis you send us.

Can the register support a lender's cut-off date?

Yes, as a record, not as a substitute. A count of the structures inside the corridor on dated imagery supports the cut-off-date record and shows what appeared afterwards. The census, the asset inventory and the consultation with households stay with the project and its resettlement consultants.

Do you inspect the track, bridges or embankments?

No. We do no engineering inspection. We map what changes at the surface, such as structures, cleared ground, tracks, excavations and areas reached by water after a flood, so field teams know where to start.

Do you need drones?

Not to start. Satellite screening covers the whole line with no flights. Where a stretch needs an orthophoto, we propose a drone survey, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires, starting with ANAC’s special authorisation.

Send us the line or road alignment

KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage, or the coordinates of stations and kilometre posts. Tell us the reserve width and what the record is for, and we reply with a written proposal.
